clue.text: All of a sudden changed partly, but not completely

indicators.note: changed tells us the letters of partly plus the shortened but are put into a new order
not completely means the word but loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Something altered only in part, and not even fully, as if someone quibbled about a sudden shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not completely' cuts BUT to BU; 'changed' then rearranges PARTLY plus BU.
explanation.definitionFit: Abruptly means suddenly and without warning, a synonym of the adverbial phrase.

clue.text: What's particularly clear in one artist

parts.note: from the simile clear as a bell
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Something especially lucid found in a single painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Bellini was a Venetian Renaissance painter.

clue.text: Upstart god gets tricked in Hindu scriptures

parts.note: read as up start: the start of the word up is its first letter, U
Pan is the Greek god of shepherds
is had means is fooled or deceived

explanation.surface: A jumped-up deity is duped in sacred Indian texts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstart' splits as 'Up start', the start of UP being U. 'Had' means fooled, so 'gets tricked' gives IS HAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upanishads are philosophical texts of Hinduism, part of the Vedas.

clue.text: Little Tommy's grub

definitions.meaning: the surname of the nursery-rhyme boy who sings for his supper

explanation.surface: A small boy's food.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Tommy Tucker is a British nursery rhyme; tucker is Australian slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the rhyme character's surname and informal Australian and British slang for food.

clue.text: How to break off official communications

definitions.text: How to break off official communications

parts.words: How to break off official communications
parts.note: not stopping talks, but the formal phrase used to sign off a business letter

explanation.surface: A guide to severing diplomatic relations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break off' suggests ending relations; it means ending a letter, the sign-off used when the recipient is addressed as Sir or Madam.
explanation.definitionFit: This valediction is the conventional close of a formal letter begun 'Dear Sir'.

clue.text: No alcoholic drink allowed in holiday house

parts.note: cha is tea, a drink with no alcohol in it
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: A dry holiday cottage where no booze is permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is an informal British word for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a wooden cottage of the Swiss type, often let to holidaymakers.

clue.text: Singularly useless Spanish instrument

parts.note: singularly is read as in the singular: a percussion piece that only works as a clicked pair

explanation.surface: A remarkably ineffective musical instrument from Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singularly' seems to mean remarkably; it means one on its own, since these clappers are played in pairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A castanet is one of a pair of wooden shells clicked together in flamenco dancing.

clue.text: Doesn't 14 make up lies? Rot!

indicators.note: make up tells us the letters of lies and rot are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being accused of fabricating stories: nonsense!
explanation.walkthrough: 14 across is MAKE HASTE, so 'Doesn't 14' means dawdles. The 'make' in 'make up' is the anagram signal, not part of 14.
explanation.definitionFit: To loiter is to linger idly, the opposite of hurrying.

clue.text: Sixty in MCC total is one's contribution to score

definitions.meaning: MCC as Roman numerals is 1200, and 60 is this fraction of it
a score is 20, so one makes up this fraction of it

explanation.surface: A batsman's sixty in a Marylebone Cricket Club innings total.
explanation.walkthrough: MCC is the Marylebone Cricket Club, but here it is the Roman numeral 1200; a score is twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: Both 60 out of 1200 and 1 out of 20 are the same fraction, one part in twenty.

clue.text: Such verses form chapter used in a secular setting

indicators.note: used in signals that the abbreviation for chapter is placed within the word for secular

parts.note: laic means lay or secular, not of the clergy

explanation.surface: A verse form whose chapter is set within a non-religious context.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' simply completes the picture of C sitting inside A LAIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcaic verses are a classical stanza form named after the Greek poet Alcaeus.

clue.text: Nursing sister's order

parts.note: read not as a command from a ward sister but as the religious order to which a nun (a sister) belongs, named after a saint

explanation.surface: An instruction given by a nursing sister on a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sister' in religious use means a nun; 'order' is a community of nuns, here the one founded in honour of Saint Ursula.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ursulines are an order of Roman Catholic nuns devoted to teaching and care, founded in 1535.

clue.text: Minc's reduced by one, with absence of Ruth

parts.note: a mine is a pit, the 's being 'is' joining it to what follows
the Roman numeral for one is I
reduced means made less, giving the word less

explanation.surface: A mine shrinks by one, and some woman named Ruth has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth' is not a woman but the old word for pity or compassion, as in ruthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth is an archaic noun for compassion, so being without it means being merciless.

clue.text: Sign of grave stress, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the grave is a written mark over a vowel, as in French
emphasis on a syllable when speaking is one example

explanation.surface: A gravestone marking some deep emotional pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grave' tempts as a burial place or seriousness; it is the backward-sloping mark on a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a diacritic mark and vocal emphasis on a syllable are senses of the same noun.

clue.text: Suspicious of a fluke, for example

definitions.meaning: a fluke is a flatfish, so this means relating to such creatures

explanation.surface: Something that happened by lucky chance looks dubious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fluke' reads as a lucky chance but is a flounder.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both questionable and like or relating to marine creatures with fins.

clue.text: It's expected to be placed in Leicester, say

definitions.text: It's expected to be placed in Leicester, say

parts.words: It's expected to be placed in Leicester, say
parts.note: placed is the racing sense of finishing in the first few, and Leicester is a racecourse town

explanation.surface: Something due to be put somewhere in an English Midlands city.
explanation.walkthrough: Leicester has a racecourse; a horse is 'placed' if it finishes second or third, as the betting's choice is expected to.
explanation.definitionFit: The favourite is the horse with the shortest odds, the one punters most expect to do well.

clue.text: What leaders of his army, seeing the enemy, do in hurry

parts.note: the leading letters make or do a word, so do stands for make

indicators.note: the leaders of the five words are their opening letters, which form a word

explanation.surface: A general describes what an army's officers do on sighting the foe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' sound like officers but are first letters of 'his army seeing the enemy', which make HASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: To make haste is an idiom meaning to rush or go quickly.

clue.text: Greek statesman is tried as crook

indicators.note: crook means bent or twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Greek politician is put on trial as a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a criminal; it means bent, rearranging IS TRIED AS. Aristides 'the Just' was an Athenian statesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristides was an Athenian general and statesman of the fifth century BC.

clue.text: Put on show having been vetted

definitions.meaning: projected on a cinema screen or broadcast

explanation.surface: A film shown after passing inspection.
explanation.definitionFit: The past participle covers both showing a film and checking a person for security.

clue.text: Justify return of police in native riot

indicators.note: in places the turned police letters inside the rearranged native
riot suggests disorder, so the letters of native are thrown into a new arrangement
return of means the police abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British plain-clothes police

explanation.surface: Police come back to deal with a disturbance among locals and claim justification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'native riot' looks like an uprising of locals, but 'riot' is the anagram signal; CID, read backwards after 'return of', sits inside the reshuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To vindicate is to clear or show to be right, a synonym of justify.

clue.text: Like Mrs. Malaprop's allegory, nothing to do with ears

definitions.note: Mrs Malaprop says headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile, meaning an alligator

parts.note: nil means nothing or zero
otic is the medical adjective for the ear

explanation.surface: A garbled figure of speech has nothing to do with listening.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's The Rivals, Mrs Malaprop calls Lydia 'as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means of the Nile river, home of the crocodile-like creature she meant.

clue.text: Jollity present in Twelfth Night

parts.note: alludes to Feste's song in Shakespeare's comedy, which sings of present merriment having present laughter

explanation.surface: Fun on hand during the festive twelfth night of Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'O Mistress Mine' in Twelfth Night says 'Present mirth hath present laughter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirth is merriment and gaiety, a synonym of jollity, and the word appears in that very song.

clue.text: Stuff to eat, perhaps, after second half of 23

indicators.note: second half of means the final four of the eight letters of 23 across

parts.note: 23 across is Shakespeare's fat knight

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters of eat could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Food to be eaten after half a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' is the old word for cloth, not a verb; 'perhaps' rearranges EAT to ETA.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuff is old-fashioned for woven fabric, and taffeta is a crisp silk fabric.

clue.text: Beldame's reticule

definitions.meaning: a beldame is an ugly old woman; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: An old woman's handbag.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for an unpleasant elderly woman and, literally, a worn handbag.

clue.text: What leaks out from full agenda

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the run of words full agenda

explanation.surface: Something seeping out of a packed meeting schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Ullage is the amount lost from a cask or bottle by leakage or evaporation.

clue.text: Sir John swims initially in two rivers

indicators.note: in puts the opening letter of swims between the two river names

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
the Taff is a river in Wales, flowing through Cardiff

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of swims is used

explanation.surface: A knight goes for a swim, wading first into one river and then another.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is the fat knight of Shakespeare's Henry IV plays.

clue.text: Doctor meets almost all such injuries

definitions.note: the adjective is defined by the noun it describes: injuries of this kind

parts.note: an intern is a junior hospital doctor

indicators.note: almost means the word all loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written before shortening

explanation.surface: A doctor sees nearly every patient with this sort of injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such injuries' points to the adjective that goes with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Internal injuries are those to organs inside the body, the adjective filling the 'such' slot.

clue.text: Mole's ally is in torment

definitions.meaning: in The Wind in the Willows, Mole's gruff friend is a black-and-white burrowing animal

explanation.surface: A mole's friend is in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: Mole, Ratty and Toad's wise friend in Kenneth Grahame's children's book is this animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal name is also a verb meaning to pester or nag relentlessly.

clue.text: Outdo former tennis star, say

indicators.note: say means the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: an ex-seed, a player formerly seeded in a tournament

explanation.surface: Beating a retired tennis champion.
explanation.walkthrough: A seed is a top-ranked player in a tennis draw; ex- marks former.
explanation.definitionFit: To exceed is to go beyond or surpass, a synonym of outdo.

clue.text: Does European find new V. & A. so ugly?

indicators.note: new signals that the letters V, A and so ugly are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: A stands for itself, as printed
V stands for itself, as printed

explanation.surface: Does a visitor from the continent think the Victoria and Albert Museum is hideous?
explanation.walkthrough: 'V. & A.' looks like the London museum but just supplies V and A to rearrange with SO UGLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yugoslav was a citizen of the former Balkan federation, a European nationality.
